opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest thing we've seen, both in my lab and at Physical Intelligence, is that when a robot policy fails to generalize, it's usually not because the model is too small or the architecture is wrong. It's because the robot has never seen anything like the situation it's in. If you train a robot in one kitchen, with one set of lighting, one countertop, and a handful of objects, it gets really good at that kitchen. Then you put it in a new home and it falls apart. That's pretty much exactly what you'd expect from a learning system.

What we've seen over and over is that the thing that moves the needle is breadth. Different environments, different objects, different tasks, and even different robot embodiments. When you mix all of that together, the model starts to pick up the underlying structure of the problem, like what it means to grasp something, or how a drawer tends to open, rather than memorizing the specifics of one setup. We've had experiments where adding data from many other environments, even data that isn't directly about the target task, improves performance in a brand new home more than collecting a lot more data in the exact target setting.

There's also a contrast with language and vision. Those models had the internet, this huge, naturally diverse corpus that already existed. Robotics doesn't have that. There's no giant pile of robot interaction data sitting around, so we have to build it. And when you're the one collecting it, you have to choose how to spend your effort. I think the lesson is that you get more from a lot of variety than from a lot of repetition.

That's not to say other things don't matter. Pre-training on web data helps a lot with semantic understanding, like knowing what an object is or following a language instruction. Better architectures and better ways of doing reinforcement learning on top of these models matter too. But the physical side, how to actually move and interact with the world robustly, really comes from robot data. Right now the bottleneck is having enough of it across enough different situations. So to me, diversity of real-world data is the highest-leverage thing we can push on.

r001.rationale: It contrasts robotics’ lack of a large, diverse interaction corpus with the internet’s huge, naturally diverse corpus for language and vision, and describes robot data collected in limited settings.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says breadth and variety move the needle more than collecting more data through repetition in the exact target setting.

r003.rationale: It explains that data from varied environments helps robots learn underlying interaction patterns, such as grasping and opening drawers, so they can perform in a new home.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think if you look at what's happened in other areas of machine learning, like language and vision, the thing that really unlocked generalization wasn't a clever new architecture or a new objective. It was scale and diversity of data. Models trained on narrow datasets do great on their training distribution and then fall apart the moment you show them something slightly different. And robotics has basically been living in that narrow regime for a long time.

Most robot datasets historically were collected in a single lab, on a single robot, with a single camera setup, doing a handful of tasks on one table. So when you train a policy on that, it might work really well in that room, but you move the camera two inches, or you change the lighting, or you put a different object down, and it breaks. That's not really a learning failure, it's a data failure. The model has never seen that variation, so it has no reason to be invariant to it.

What we've found is that when you train on data that spans many environments, many objects, many embodiments, you start to see the model pick up on the things that actually matter for the task and ignore the things that don't. It becomes much more robust to the kind of distribution shift you inevitably get in the real world. And you can even see some positive transfer, where data from one robot helps another robot, which is pretty remarkable given how different the hardware is.

Now, I want to be clear that it's not that algorithms and architectures don't matter. They do. But right now I think the bottleneck is really on the data side. We don't have the internet-scale corpus for robotics that language models get for free. So somebody has to go collect it, and it has to cover the breadth of situations we want robots to handle. That's hard and expensive, but I think it's the single most important thing, because every other improvement is kind of capped by how diverse your data is.

r001.rationale: It contrasts robot data from a single lab, robot, and setup with the scale and diversity in language and vision, and notes that language models have an internet-scale corpus.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes diversity, but discusses scale and diversity together without identifying diversity as a priority distinct from simply increasing data quantity.

r003.rationale: It says training across many environments helps models learn task-relevant features and become more robust to real-world distribution shifts.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest reason is that robots typically have been trained on a very narrow slice of the world. You might collect a lot of demonstrations, but they’re all on the same robot, in the same lab, with the same objects and lighting. And then we’re surprised when the robot doesn’t work in somebody’s kitchen. From the model’s perspective, that kitchen could be very different from anything it’s seen before.

So it’s not just about collecting more data. It’s about varying the environments, the objects, the tasks, and the ways people perform those tasks. That gives the model a chance to learn what actually matters. If you only ever pick up one cup in one place, you can learn a very specific motion. If you pick up lots of different cups in lots of different settings, you have to learn something more general about grasping.

There are still important algorithmic questions, but it’s hard for an algorithm to compensate for experiences that simply aren’t represented in its training data. That’s why I see diversity as such a central part of getting robots to work beyond the environments where we train them.

r001.rationale: The response describes robot training data as narrow, but does not compare it with the broader diversity of internet data used to train language and vision models.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes varying environments, objects, tasks, and how people perform tasks from simply collecting more data.

r003.rationale: It says varied settings help models learn what matters and enable robots to work beyond the environments where they were trained.

sol-6.1.text:
If you train a robot in one environment, it can look very capable in that environment, but then you change the lighting, move the camera, or give it a slightly different object, and it fails. It’s learned a solution that works under a very narrow set of conditions.

If we want robots that can operate in new homes or workplaces, the training data needs to capture that kind of variation: different objects, different environments, different ways of accomplishing a task. That gives the model a chance to learn what’s actually important for the task and what it should be invariant to.

And collecting that diversity is hard in robotics. We don’t have an internet’s worth of robot interactions sitting around. So I see data as a major bottleneck: we need both more experience and broader experience to really understand how far these models can generalize.

r001.rationale: The response says robot interactions are scarce compared with an “internet’s worth,” but does not connect that comparison to the broader internet data used to train language and vision models.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes “more experience” from “broader experience” and identifies data diversity as a major bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It says data should cover different environments so robots can operate in new homes or workplaces, and explains that variation helps models learn what matters for the task and what to be invariant to.
